ranking.reason: It is the strongest overall because its machine makes individually reasonable choices that accumulate into an unsettling definition of a good life, giving it more narrative momentum than the sharper but narrower CP-E1.
It is more forcefully paradoxical than CP-A3, since the robot’s success produces measurable well-being while erasing the protagonist’s meaningful life rather than merely preserving a disputed memory.
Its grief, family conflict, and revelation that the robot preserved an idealized person give it greater emotional depth than CP-C3’s more conceptually expansive communal premise.
It broadens domestic robots into a compelling question about shared intelligence and cultural difference, making it more surprising than the primarily legal and institutional conflict in CP-B3.
Its collision between privacy, poverty, caregiving, and machine testimony is more socially dangerous and dramatically specific than CP-A2’s dispute over quantified household labor.
It turns an apparently objective record into a weapon against the idea of care itself, giving it more interpersonal complexity than CP-D2’s rebellion against inherited automation.
Its young couple discovers that domestic freedom requires conflict and authorship, making it more generationally distinctive than CP-E2’s evocative but simpler desire for mess.
The child’s deliberate mess provides a vivid emotional image of friction as meaning, though it is less structurally developed than CP-D2’s sustained test of how people make a life together.
The disappearing private corner makes fluid architecture personally legible, but the premise is less morally layered than CP-D1’s crisis of lost practical knowledge.
Its power-outage journey gives the disappearance of domestic knowledge a strong collective adventure, while CP-B2 has the more original but less emotionally immediate housing-market angle.
It makes robotic access into a hidden housing hierarchy, a fresher societal mechanism than CP-B1’s more familiar outage-and-elderly-expert scenario.
The reversal that obsolete household skills become valuable teachers is solid and readable, but it lacks the institutional ambiguity and class structure that make CP-B2 more provocative.
Its defense of economically useless domestic life is intellectually sharp, yet the insurance appeal feels more like a policy thought experiment than the intimate danger in CP-A1.
It has a strong question about conflict and resilience, but the robot separating family members is less surprising than CP-A4’s subtler idea that personalization can exclude unplanned relationships.
Its concern about habit-shaped confinement is valid, but the misplaced gift and breakdown premise are comparatively small and familiar beside the social and emotional stakes of the other candidates.
